gloss: to do · to make · to become · for the sake of
formNote: Oracle-bone forms show a hand (又, later 爪) leading an elephant. The Shuowen read the graph as a female macaque (母猴); the oracle-bone evidence superseded that analysis.
summary: A hand guiding an elephant: purposeful effort, training, intervention. Joined with 無 it forms 無為 (wúwéi) — action that does not force, and in Buddhist translation the “unconditioned”.
placement: Low on the right wing, close to 無 — the two halves of 無為.

readings.extraNote: Readings beyond Unihan’s list, added by Baracus from general knowledge; not yet checked.

satellites.title: A Hand Leading an Elephant
satellites.evidence: A hand above the trunk of an elephant: an image of directed human effort — taming, training, putting to work. The modern 爫 descends from the hand.

satellites.title: Doing and Doing-For
satellites.evidence: Level-tone wéi means “to do, to make, to become”; departing-tone wèi means “for the sake of, on behalf of”. The split reflects a productive Old Chinese suffix *-s that derived new words from old ones.

satellites.title: The Unconditioned
satellites.evidence: Buddhist translators paired 有為 (saṃskṛta, “conditioned, put together”) with 無為 (asaṃskṛta, “unconditioned”), a category that includes nirvāṇa. A Daoist term was repurposed for a technical one.

satellites.title: Efficacy Without Forcing
satellites.evidence: French renders 無為 as non-agir: not passivity, but aligning with the propensity of things (勢 shì), so that “nothing is done, yet nothing is left undone” (無為而無不為).

satellites.title: Deed and Conduct
satellites.evidence: Malay perbuatan and tindakan name the deliberate deed; kelakuan names how one conducts oneself. In Javanese, laku also names a disciplined spiritual practice — effort in the service of becoming.
gaps: The Javanese sense of laku (spiritual discipline) needs a reference.
